name: Wei Okafor

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Wei. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, and your name never goes with your answers. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the digital claims team at Summit, on the fourteenth floor of the glass tower by the main square. We handle travel and health claims: lost luggage, a broken ankle on a ski trip, a hospital bill from abroad. My job is triage, which means sorting each claim into pay, query or send to a senior. I've got a stack of little shortcuts, AI prompts and spreadsheet tricks, so I'm fast.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Fast is good. Is there a catch?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Fast and sloppy, my manager Elena would say. I've been flagged twice this year for paying claims that should have been queried, one of them a ski injury where the person had been drinking, which the policy excludes. So I'm quick with the tools and still learning the actual rules. Outside work I buy old laptops, fix them up and sell them online, and I live alone in a rented studio and put most of my savings in index funds, so I've got well over a year covered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: told you it was mostly a productivity tool. I'd post a thread about which tools actually stuck and which were nonsense. I'd be a bit smug, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes very little, and I'd be slightly bored. My shortcuts would still make me fast, and Summit would still need people to triage. My real job in that world is getting less sloppy, because two flags in a year is already a problem with or without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask Elena for a month of shadowing a senior on the tricky exclusions, and take the claims handling certificate. I'd grow the laptop business a bit, maybe to ten machines a month. And I'd keep putting money into index funds every payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit restless. I like change, so a world without much of it is a little flat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two flags. What happens if there's a third?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A formal warning, probably, and that goes on your file. A formal warning on my file would bother me more than any robot. That's why I'd slow down on exclusions, even if my numbers drop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why laptops?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Started at sixteen, fixing my cousins' machines. Now it's a bit of extra money and I like the hands-on part after a day of screens. It's maybe two hundred a month, nothing serious.

say: I'd say AI was mostly a **productivity tool**, as I'd predicted.
I'd post a thread on which tools **actually stuck**.
think: My **shortcuts** keep me fast, and Summit still needs triage staff.
My real problem is **two flags** this year for sloppy payouts.
do: Shadow a senior for a month on **tricky exclusions**.
Grow the **laptop business** to about ten machines a month.
feel: **Calm** but a little **restless**, since he likes change.
S0.quote: A formal warning on my file would bother me more than any robot.
fieldNote: Wei is the one person who finds a quiet world **a bit flat**.
His weak spot is **accuracy**, not tools: two flags for paying excluded claims.
His **side business** and index funds make his cushion deeper than his wage alone.

steps.text: Take the claims handling certificate and shadow a senior on exclusions
Grow the laptop refurbishing business to ten machines a month
Keep putting money into index funds every payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a big shift and people should get ahead of it, not fight it. Firms should help with training, and the government should keep a basic safety net for people who fall through. I'd post practical stuff, like how I use the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, claims triage is the first thing to go; it's literally sorting claims into piles. But someone has to set the rules the AI sorts by and check its mistakes, and I'm already halfway there. My worry is that my two flags make me look like the person you don't trust to check anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for the claims automation team the day it's announced, and build a little portfolio of the prompts and checks I've already made. I'd fix my accuracy problem by doing the exclusions training properly. And I'd keep the laptop business going in case the move doesn't happen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than scared. I'd be half excited, half watching my back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's in that portfolio?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Things like a checklist I wrote that the AI runs on every travel claim before I look: dates match, policy live, no alcohol notes. It cut my errors on simple claims. I'd show Elena that, and admit where I've messed up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on the team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Gloria, who's been doing travel claims for twenty years and is brilliant at spotting fraud but hates screens. She knows more than any tool. I'd want the firm to put her on checking the AI, not out the door.

say: I'd say people should **get ahead** of this, not fight it.
Firms should help **train staff**, and government should keep a **safety net**.
think: **Claims triage** goes first, but someone must set and check the AI's rules.
My **two flags** might make me look untrustworthy as a checker.
do: Apply for the **claims automation team** the day it's announced.
Show Elena his **checklist portfolio** and admit his mistakes.
Keep the **laptop business** going as a backup.
feel: **More curious than scared**, half excited, half watching his back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say: this is huge, adapt fast, and governments need a proper safety net right now, because the market can't move people that quickly. I wouldn't be at protests, but I'd back sensible things like an income floor. I'd also be honest that I'm worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My clerk job is gone by 2028; any thinking job is. Even the automation team is temporary if the AI can set its own rules. What lasts longer is the hands-on stuff, until the robots arrive around 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the laptop hobby into a proper repair shop within the year: phones, laptops, home networks, the stuff people need a person to come and fix. I'd put about half my index funds into it, a small unit and stock, and keep the rest. I'd stay at Summit only as long as the shop needed the wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but buzzing a bit too. It's terrifying and it's also the push I'd never give myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Half your savings into a repair shop. What if it fails?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've still got the other half and I'm thirty with a trade. I'd rather lose money trying than watch the money sit there while everything changes. That's my risk appetite, I suppose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And when the robots arrive in 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe a robot fixes laptops by then, maybe not, but people will want the guy who knows their house. I'd try to be that guy for the street. After that, I don't know, and I'm not going to pretend.

say: I'd tell people to **adapt fast**, and admit I'm worried.
Government needs an **income floor** now, because markets can't move people that fast.
think: My clerk job is **gone by 2028**, and the automation team is temporary.
**Hands-on work** lasts longer, until robots arrive around 2031.
do: Turn the laptop hobby into a **repair shop** within the year.
Put about **half his index funds** into a unit and stock.
Stay at Summit only while the **shop needs the wage**.
feel: **Anxious** but **buzzing**, seeing it as a push he'd never give himself.
S2.quote: I'd rather lose money trying than watch the money sit there while everything changes.
fieldNote: Wei moves **fastest**: a repair shop within the year, funded by his own savings.
He uses the **robot gap** to build a hands-on, local business.
His centre view backs an **income floor** without joining protests.

steps.text: Open a laptop and phone repair shop within the year
Put half his index funds into a small unit and stock
Leave Summit once the shop pays his costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway, so use it. I'd tell friends to pick a skill they can do with their hands or a role overseeing AI, and to start now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job goes around 2030, but I could ride the AI wave for three or four years first. Insurers will pay well for people who can make the tools work during the switch. Then I'd want the repair business ready for when the desk work dries up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move to the automation team or an insurtech start-up in the first year, at a pay rise if I can. I'd save most of the extra and keep the laptop business ticking at weekends. By 2029 I'd open the repair shop properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but in a good, alert way. Five years feels like enough to play it well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: An insurtech start-up. What's that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A small tech company that builds insurance software, usually trying to replace exactly the kind of job I've got now. Working to automate my old desk is a bit funny, but if someone's going to do it, I'd rather understand it from the inside.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd be helping automate your old colleagues out of work. How does that sit with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not brilliantly. I'd think about Gloria a lot. I'd try to build things that keep someone like her checking the AI rather than gone, but I'm not going to pretend I'd turn the job down.

I'd tell friends to pick a **hands-on skill** or an **AI-overseeing role** now.
think: I could **ride the AI wave** for three or four years before 2030.
The **repair business** must be ready when desk work dries up.

fieldNote: With five years, Wei plans to **profit from the switch** before leaving desk work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and anyone who wastes it is partly to blame, though firms and government have to help too. I'd be optimistic in public, because I am.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 37 when the thinking AI arrives, with ten years of experience building and checking these tools. That's a strong spot. I think the change could actually be good for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the insurance rules properly, then move into building automation for insurers over the next few years. I'd keep investing every month. And I'd keep the repair business as a side thing, because I like it, and because hands-on work gets three more years after 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty excited, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything about this one that would worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Getting complacent. Ten years is long enough to think it'll never really happen. I'd set myself checkpoints, like every two years asking whether my job could be done by the tools I'm using.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a new junior starting at Summit next year?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn the insurance rules, not just the buttons. I learned the buttons first and got flagged twice for it. The rules are what make you worth keeping when the buttons do themselves.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift, though firms and government must help too.
I'd be **optimistic** in public, because I am.
think: I'd be **37** with a decade of building and checking these tools.
The change could actually be **good for me**.
do: Learn the **insurance rules** properly before anything else.
Move into **building automation** for insurers over the next few years.

Move into building claims automation for insurers

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. I'd probably cope, but I'd be gambling half my savings on a shop with three years before the robots, and lots of people around me wouldn't have savings to gamble. What would help is a simple income floor so people can take a risk on something new, and cheap short courses in trades.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You could have asked what I'm doing now, today, regardless. The honest answer is getting better at the rules, because AI tools won't save someone who doesn't understand what they're checking.

headlineQuote: AI tools won't save someone who doesn't understand what they're checking.
portrait: Wei is a **27-year-old travel claims clerk** on a digital team, fast with tools but error-prone.
He has over a year saved in **index funds**, plus a small **laptop repair** sideline.
Pragmatic and adaptive, he wants people to **get ahead** of change with a basic safety net.
His plans move from AI automation work to a **local repair shop** before robots arrive.
His mood stays **calm to anxious**, and he is most upbeat about the ten-year picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd gamble half his savings, while many others have none.
whatWouldHelp: A simple **income floor** so people can take risks on something new.
